title: What If You Used 100% of Your Brain?
description: You've heard you only use 10% of your brain. So what would happen if you switched on the rest? Superpowers, mind reading, perfect memory, total body control: we go through the questions everyone secretly asks, and answer them honestly with science. Every claim is sourced below.
sources: Azevedo et al. (2009), Equal numbers of neuronal and nonneuronal cells make the human brain an isometrically scaled-up primate brain, J Comp Neurol. https://doi.org/10.1002/cne.21974
Raichle & Gusnard (2002), Appraising the brain's energy budget, PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.172399499
Lennie (2003), The cost of cortical computation, Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0960-9822(03)00135-0
James, W. (1907), The Energies of Men, Science 25:321-332.
Hochberg et al. (2012), Reach and grasp by people with tetraplegia using a neurally controlled robotic arm, Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11076
Parker, Cahill & McGaugh (2006), A case of unusual autobiographical remembering, Neurocase. https://doi.org/10.1080/13554790500473680
Treffert (2014), Savant syndrome: realities, myths and misconceptions, J Autism Dev Disord. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-013-1897-z
Kox et al. (2014), Voluntary activation of the sympathetic nervous system and attenuation of the innate immune response in humans, PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1322174111
Wager et al. (2004), Placebo-induced changes in fMRI in the anticipation and experience of pain, Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1093065

scenes.narration: You've probably heard it. You only use ten percent of your brain.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) on a cosy sofa at night, a transparent head showing the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome with only a few windows lit

scenes.narration: And honestly? It's a tempting idea. Somewhere inside your skull, ninety percent of you is just... asleep. Waiting for someone to flip the switch.
scenes.image_prompt: a giant old-fashioned power switch inside the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome, most of the city dark and sleeping, a tiny figure looking up at the switch

scenes.narration: Movies love it. One pill, one strange accident, and suddenly you learn languages in an afternoon, read minds, and move things with a glance.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) swallowing a glowing pill, books and objects floating around them, dramatic cinema-poster lighting

scenes.narration: So what would really happen if you woke it all up? Would you get superpowers? Could you control your own body? Would you remember every single breakfast you've ever had?
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) surrounded by floating thought bubbles: a lightning bolt, a heart, a stack of breakfast plates going up to the sky

scenes.narration: This is your brain. At one hundred percent.
scenes.image_prompt: the green glass planet Mindsphere with a glowing orbit ring in space, a bright brain-shaped city glowing on its surface, epic title composition

scenes.narration: Before we start: brains are the most complicated objects we know of, so we're simplifying a lot. Every study we mention is linked in the description.
scenes.image_prompt: Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) holding up a small glass sign next to a stack of science journals, friendly wink

scenes.narration: Inside your head sit about eighty-six billion neurons. If each one were a person, your brain could hold the population of more than ten Earths.
scenes.image_prompt: ten small blue-green Earths lined up in a row, each full of tiny glowing dots like people

scenes.narration: Each neuron is connected to thousands of others, through tiny gaps called synapses. Together they form something like a city. A city of light.
scenes.image_prompt: two glowing neurons reaching toward each other with a tiny sparkling gap between them, a city skyline of neurons behind

scenes.narration: Picture it at night. Roads of nerve fibres. Districts for seeing, hearing, moving and feeling. And in every window, a neuron that can switch its light on.
scenes.image_prompt: wide aerial view of the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome, districts with little glass signs shaped like an eye, an ear, a hand and a heart, roads of light between them

scenes.narration: Your brain makes up only about two percent of your body weight. But it burns around twenty percent of your energy. It is, by far, the most expensive thing you own.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) holding a tiny brain on one side of a balance scale, a huge pile of food and batteries on the other side

scenes.narration: So does this city really sit ninety percent dark? Let's check.
scenes.image_prompt: Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) with a flashlight peeking into a dark street of the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome

scenes.narration: Nobody knows exactly where the myth began. It's often blamed on the psychologist William James, who wrote that we use only a small part of our possible mental resources. Which is not the same thing at all.
scenes.image_prompt: an old 1900s study room with a bearded scholar writing at a desk by lamp light, papers flying, sepia accents

scenes.narration: Self-help books loved the idea, and turned a vague sentence into a hard number. Ten percent.
scenes.image_prompt: a pile of colourful self-help books with a giant glowing 10% sign rising from them like a neon advert

scenes.narration: But brain scans disagree. Watch a brain over a single day, and practically every region lights up at some point. There is no silent ninety percent.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) lying in a friendly glass brain scanner, a holographic brain above them lit up in many colourful patches

scenes.narration: And evolution would never allow it. Remember, the brain is wildly expensive. Carrying around ninety percent dead weight that eats energy? Natural selection would have thrown it out long ago.
scenes.image_prompt: a stone-age family by a campfire, one person carrying a huge heavy glowing backpack labelled with a brain icon, looking exhausted

scenes.narration: Even small injuries prove the point. Damage almost any part of the brain, even a tiny one, and something changes. Speech, memory, movement, personality.
scenes.image_prompt: one small district of the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome going dark like a power cut, with little icons for speech, memory and movement flickering out

scenes.narration: So the truth is: you already use all of your brain. Just not all at the same time.
scenes.image_prompt: the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome where lights switch on in different districts in a gentle wave, like a living map

scenes.narration: Right now, as you watch this, your seeing district decodes the picture. Your language areas turn my words into meaning. And somewhere, a quiet part checks whether you're hungry.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) watching a screen, three glowing districts of their brain highlighted: an eye district, a speech-bubble district and a tiny kitchen with a sandwich

scenes.narration: Most windows in the city are dark at any moment. And that is not a flaw. It's the design.
scenes.image_prompt: close-up of a building in the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome with only a few warm windows lit, calm and peaceful

scenes.narration: Energy is the reason. Your cortex can only afford to keep a small fraction of its neurons highly active at once. Some estimates say around one percent.
scenes.image_prompt: a glowing power meter beside the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome with only a thin slice filled, Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) pointing at it

scenes.narration: Your brain doesn't work by switching everything on. It works by choosing which few lights matter right now.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) holding a glowing lantern on a dark city street, choosing one bright path among many

scenes.narration: So what if we ignored all that, and flipped every switch in the city at the same time? Spoiler: it does not end with superpowers. It ends with a blackout.
scenes.image_prompt: the giant power switch in the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome being pushed up, the whole city flashing white too bright, sparks flying

scenes.narration: Let's go through the questions everyone secretly asks. Starting with the big one.
scenes.image_prompt: Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) holding a big glass question mark in front of the Mindsphere planet

scenes.narration: What if all your neurons fired at once? We actually know what that looks like. When huge groups of neurons fire together, out of control, the result is a seizure.
scenes.image_prompt: the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome with every light flashing in sync like a strobe, wavy lines of electricity across the sky

scenes.narration: Not genius. Not telekinesis. The lights all flash together, the signals turn into noise, and for a moment nothing makes sense at all.
scenes.image_prompt: a radio tower in the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome sending out scrambled static waves, letters and symbols breaking apart

scenes.narration: Okay. But could you read minds? Sadly, no. No study has ever shown reliable telepathy.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) and a friend facing each other with antenna headbands, a thought bubble between them showing only a big question mark, funny mood

scenes.narration: But moving things with your thoughts? That one is surprisingly real. With a small brain implant, people who are paralysed have controlled computer cursors and even robotic arms, just by imagining the movement.
scenes.image_prompt: a person in a wheelchair smiling as a sleek robotic arm lifts a cup of coffee, glowing signal lines from their head to the arm

scenes.narration: No pill. No secret ninety percent. Just a very clever translator between the city's lights and a machine.
scenes.image_prompt: a tiny glass translator device turning glowing city lights into robot gears and signals, Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) watching curiously

scenes.narration: What about remembering everything? A few dozen people on Earth come close. They have something called highly superior autobiographical memory. Name any date, and they can tell you what day of the week it was, and what they did.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) standing in an endless glass library of calendars and diaries, one date page glowing

scenes.narration: Sounds amazing, right? But the first person studied described it as a burden. Every embarrassing moment, every loss, replayed in full colour. Forgetting, it turns out, is a gift.
scenes.image_prompt: a person sitting on a bench surrounded by too many floating memory screens, looking tired, soft rain

scenes.narration: Then there are savants. Stephen Wiltshire can fly over a city once, and then draw its skyline in astonishing detail from memory.
scenes.image_prompt: an artist drawing a huge detailed city skyline on a long sheet of paper, a helicopter in the sky behind

scenes.narration: And in rare cases, such talents appear suddenly. After a head injury, a handful of people have woken up with new skills, like playing the piano, that they never had before.
scenes.image_prompt: a person in a hospital bed looking surprised as glowing piano keys appear in the air in front of them

scenes.narration: Scientists think this may happen when some brain areas grow quieter, and others get room to shine. Again: not more brain. A different balance.
scenes.image_prompt: the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome where one district dims and the neighbouring district glows brighter, like a seesaw of light

scenes.narration: Could you control your body with your mind? Partly. In one study, volunteers trained in breathing techniques and cold exposure were given a bacterial toxin, and had far fewer flu-like symptoms than untrained people.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) breathing calmly in an icy blue lake, glowing shield shapes around them, snowy mountains

scenes.narration: And the placebo effect shows that simply expecting to feel better can really reduce pain. Your thoughts do reach your body. But you can't regrow a finger by wishing.
scenes.image_prompt: a doctor handing a sugar pill to a patient, a soft glow easing a red pain spot on their arm

scenes.narration: And feeling no pain at all? That exists too. It's rare, and it's dangerous. Children with this condition can break a bone or burn a hand without noticing. Pain is a bodyguard, not a weakness.
scenes.image_prompt: a small friendly glowing guardian figure standing protectively in front of a child near a hot stove

scenes.narration: Did you just quietly check that you can still feel your toes? Good. Your bodyguard is working.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) looking down and wiggling their toes in fuzzy socks, Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) giving a thumbs up, funny mood

scenes.narration: So: no hidden ninety percent. No superpowers waiting behind a locked door. The end. Well... almost.
scenes.image_prompt: a locked glass door in the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome with nothing behind it, Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) raising one finger with a sly look

scenes.narration: Because you do have one real superpower. And you're using it right now. Your city can rebuild itself.
scenes.image_prompt: tiny construction workers made of light building new glowing roads in the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome

scenes.narration: Scientists call it neuroplasticity. Every time you learn something, the links between neurons grow stronger. New roads appear in the city.
scenes.image_prompt: new glowing bridges forming between two districts of the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome at sunrise

scenes.narration: London taxi drivers have to memorise around twenty-five thousand streets. Brain scans showed that a part of their brain that handles navigation, the hippocampus, was larger than in other people.
scenes.image_prompt: a classic black London taxi driving through a glowing map maze, a seahorse-shaped glowing structure inside a driver's head

scenes.narration: Their brains didn't get more percent. They got better roads.
scenes.image_prompt: a small dirt path in the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome turning into a wide shining highway

scenes.narration: And you can do the same. It sounds almost too simple. But three things have strong science behind them.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) looking at three glowing glass cards floating in front of them, numbered one, two, three

scenes.narration: One: sleep. While you sleep, your brain replays the day and strengthens what matters. Skip it, and much of what you learned simply fades.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) asleep in bed under a starry window while the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome above them replays scenes of the day like little films

scenes.narration: Two: move. In one study, older adults who walked briskly three times a week for a year grew their hippocampus by about two percent. Roughly like turning the clock back by one to two years.
scenes.image_prompt: an older couple walking briskly on a green hill path at sunrise, a small glowing seahorse shape growing above them

scenes.narration: Three: learn something genuinely new. A language, an instrument, a dance. New skills build new roads, at almost any age.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) learning guitar while words in different languages and dance steps float around as glowing roads

scenes.narration: No pill. No switch. Just small things, done again and again.
scenes.image_prompt: a single glowing footstep path climbing up a gentle green hill toward the Mindsphere planet in the sky

scenes.narration: So the next time someone tells you that you only use ten percent of your brain, you can smile. Your city is already lit. Every district, every street. Just not all at once.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) smiling, behind them the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome glowing in gentle waves across all districts

scenes.narration: And that's the beautiful part. You don't need to switch everything on. You get to choose which lights to keep burning, and which new roads to build.
scenes.image_prompt: the protagonist (young person with short dark hair and a teal hoodie) placing a small glowing lamp on a new road in the brain drawn as a glowing night city inside a glass dome, warm amber light

scenes.narration: Your brain isn't waiting for an upgrade. It's waiting for you. If you'd like to explore more of the Mindsphere with us, subscribe. See you on the next orbit.
scenes.image_prompt: the green glass planet Mindsphere with its glowing orbit ring, Orbi (a small floating glass orb robot with a glowing orbit ring and two dot eyes) waving goodbye in the foreground, stars and soft lens glow
